summary: Describes use cases for measuring broadband performance across many homes and devices. Providers, users and regulators all have reasons to measure, and understanding these scenarios helped shape the LMAP framework. It is background material rather than a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Many people want to know how fast home internet really is. This explains who wants to measure it and why, so a system for measuring lots of connections can be designed.

subtitle: Why organizations measure broadband performance at scale.

tldr.problem: Network operators, regulators, and users all need to measure broadband performance reliably at scale, but lack a common framework for doing so.
tldr.mechanism: The Large-scale Measurement of Broadband Performance (LMAP) framework establishes use cases and requirements so that different organizations can deploy compatible measurement systems.
tldr.outcome: LMAP provides the foundation for standardized, interoperable broadband measurement that can support network diagnostics, regulatory oversight, and transparency for end users.

today: RFC 7536 is Informational and remains active. It defines the use cases that guide the LMAP framework, information model, and protocols being developed to enable standardized, large-scale broadband measurement.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Large-scale Measurement of Broadband Performance (LMAP) is a framework for measuring how well broadband networks actually perform. Three main groups care about these measurements: network operators (ISPs), regulators, and end users.

The RFC identifies two primary use cases. In the first, a network operator wants to understand the performance of their network and the quality experienced by customers. In the second, a regulator wants to provide transparent performance information about ISPs in their jurisdiction. Although the initial LMAP work focuses on these two cases, the mechanisms are designed to support other uses as well, such as end users measuring their own performance or identifying problems in their home networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Companies that run the internet and governments that oversee them both want to measure how fast internet really is. They measure speed, delays, and how often data gets lost, and they use this information to fix problems and help customers understand what they are paying for.

sections.title: ISP Use Cases
sections.content:
Network operators use large-scale measurements in five main ways.

Understanding customer experience: ISPs deploy measurement probes to a representative sample of customers' homes to understand Quality of Experience (QoE). A probe is software or a device that measures performance and reports results to a measurement system. The operator gains an end-to-end view by measuring from customers' homes to services across the internet, not just from their own network edge. Operators want to relate measurements to metrics like 'mean opinion score' that connect raw network numbers to actual user experience.

Testing new technology: Before rolling out IPv6, new QoS mechanisms, or other changes, operators measure their impact on a subset of customers. This helps them assess whether new technology is worth deploying widely.

Design and planning: By measuring performance at multiple points, operators identify which customer groups experience below-expected performance during peak hours. This information helps with capacity planning and network design.

Monitoring service agreements: ISPs monitor whether they meet their own Service Level Agreements (SLAs) with customers and check whether suppliers (transit operators, CDNs, peering partners) meet theirs.

Identifying problems: Large-scale measurements help operators spot faults more rapidly. While traditional network alarms trigger on outages, measurements provide a nuanced view of degradation that affects groups of customers—for example, all users connected to a particular network exchange or using a specific home gateway model. This helps operators isolate and fix problems faster.
sections.plainLanguage: ISPs use measurement to understand how satisfied customers are, test new features before rolling them out, plan network upgrades, check that suppliers keep their promises, and find network problems faster.

sections.title: Regulator Use Cases
sections.content:
Regulators have three main measurement goals.

Transparent performance information: Regulators publish performance data about Internet access services so end users can make informed choices. Published information must be accurate (reproducible and consistent), comparable (using the same metrics across ISPs and over time), meaningful (reflecting what users actually value), and reliable (based on appropriate sample sizes and statistical processing).

Measuring deployment: Regulators track whether broadband deployment improves over time, particularly where governments have set strategic goals for high-speed broadband availability.

Monitoring traffic management: Regulators monitor whether ISPs treat traffic fairly or whether they block, throttle, or prioritize certain applications. This supports net neutrality and open internet policies in jurisdictions that have adopted them.
sections.plainLanguage: Governments use measurements to tell people how fast different internet companies really are, to check if broadband is getting better over time, and to watch for unfair treatment of apps and services.

sections.title: Implementation Approaches
sections.content:
The RFC describes three main ways to deploy measurement systems, each with trade-offs.

Hardware probes: Special devices deployed to a carefully selected panel of customers perform scheduled measurements. The measurement system tightly controls when tests run and which customers are involved. This allows reliable benchmarks with relatively few devices, but deploying hardware at the scale needed for per-customer fault diagnosis is expensive.

Software applications: Users download an app or access a webpage where they can run tests on demand. The system gains scale easily because users themselves choose to participate, but the resulting measurements include the user's home network (which varies widely) and the panel is self-selecting and potentially biased. Post-processing can reduce these biases.

Embedded capability: Measurement software runs as part of a device's firmware, such as in a home gateway or mobile module. This offers a middle ground between hardware probes and apps, making it more practical to reach many users.

Regardless of approach, the measurement operator must carefully design tests to avoid harming user experience—for example, by measuring only when the user is not actively using the broadband, and by not counting measurement traffic against the user's data allowance or bill.
sections.plainLanguage: Measurement systems can use special boxes installed in homes (reliable but expensive), apps people download (easy to scale but less controlled), or software built into home routers and cellular devices (a good middle ground).

sections.title: Security and Privacy Concerns
sections.content:
Large-scale measurement systems raise significant security and privacy issues. Attackers might try to gain control of probes to launch denial-of-service attacks or to monitor users' traffic and habits. A compromised measurement system could reveal which broadband lines are being tested to a network operator trying to avoid regulation, or could change test results to distort findings.

Privacy concerns include the risk that data collected by probes reveals what websites users visit, when they are home, and where their devices are located. Networks must protect this data carefully.

Measurement operators must obtain informed user consent, clearly specify what data is collected and how it is used, and designate a responsible 'data controller' accountable for data handling. If anonymized data is shared with third parties, operators must consider the risk that the third party could re-identify individuals by combining the data with other information.
sections.plainLanguage: Measurement systems must protect against attackers controlling the probes, must keep user location and browsing information private, and must get permission from people before collecting data about their internet use.
